guide.title: 5 Hidden Household Expense Leaks in Australia (And How to Plug Them Today)
guide.intro1_html: Most Aussie households don't have a spending problem so much as a leak problem. The big, visible costs, such as rent, the mortgage or a car loan, get checked all the time. Meanwhile, dozens of small direct debits and card charges quietly drain hundreds of dollars every month without anyone noticing. Because these leaks are automatic, spread out and small on their own, they slip past even careful budgeters.
guide.intro2: The good news? Leaks are usually the easiest money to win back. Unlike cutting back on things you love, plugging a leak often means paying less for exactly the same lifestyle. Here are the five most common hidden household leaks in Australia, and the practical steps you can take today to stop each one.

leak1.title_html: 1Standby Power and Energy Plans on Autopilot
leak1.body_html: Every TV, gaming console, set-top box and phone charger left on standby draws a trickle of electricity day and night. This "phantom load" can make up around 5–10% of a home's electricity use. Add air-con cooling an empty house, a second fridge humming in the garage and old halogen downlights, and your power bill carries a lot of dead weight. Many households also sit on a plan priced at or near the Default Market Offer when cheaper market offers are available.
leak1.fix1_html: Switch devices off at the wall, or use a smart power board for the TV area and home office so idle devices shut off completely.
leak1.fix2_html: Set the air-con a degree or two closer to the outside temperature, around 24–25°C for cooling in summer and 18–20°C for heating in winter, and only run it in rooms you're using. Door seals and draught stoppers cost little.
leak1.fix3_html: Compare your plan on Energy Made Easy (or Victorian Energy Compare in Victoria) by uploading a recent bill, then ask your retailer to match the best offer before you switch.
leak1.fix4: Swap halogen downlights for LEDs, wash clothes in cold water, and if you have solar, run the dishwasher and washing machine in the middle of the day.

leak2.body_html: Netflix, Stan, Binge, Kayo, Amazon Prime, Spotify, cloud storage, gym memberships and "free trials" that quietly became paid plans add up fast. Many families carry $50–$150 a month in subscriptions they rarely use. Because each one feels cheap on its own, the total hardly ever gets looked at.
leak2.fix1_html: Pull your last three months of bank and card statements and list every recurring charge. Mark the ones you used less than twice last month.
leak2.fix2_html: Rotate streaming services instead of stacking them: subscribe to one, watch what you want, cancel and move to the next.
leak2.fix3: Check your NBN speed tier and ask your provider for their current deal, or drop to a speed you won't notice. Compare your mobile plan with cheaper providers that use the same networks.
leak2.fix4: Set a phone reminder two days before any free trial ends.

leak3.title_html: 3Food Waste and the Takeaway Premium
leak3.body_html: Households often throw away a surprising share of the food they buy, especially fruit and veg, bread and leftovers. Pre-cut produce, single-serve packs and unplanned mid-week trips to the shops all carry a convenience premium. Then there's takeaway and delivery apps: when a household spends more on Uber Eats, Menulog or DoorDash than on groceries, it's often paying several times more per meal for food it could make at home.
leak3.fix1_html: Plan meals around what's already in your fridge and freezer before writing a shopping list.
leak3.fix2: Choose home brands at Coles and Woolworths for staples, or shop at Aldi. They often cost noticeably less than big brands.
leak3.fix3: Check the weekly specials, shop once a week with a list, and plan one "leftovers night" to clear the fridge.
leak3.fix4: Swap two takeaway nights a week for quick home recipes, and prep work lunches on Sunday.

leak4.title_html: 4Petrol, Rego and Insurance on Autopilot
leak4.body_html: Petrol is one of the most changeable costs in a household budget, and habits drive it. Short, scattered trips burn far more fuel per kilometre because engines are least efficient when cold. Soft tyres, driving to work alone and filling up at the wrong point in the price cycle all add up. Insurance is the quieter twin of this leak. Car, home and contents premiums tend to creep up at every renewal, and households that never shop around can pay more than they need to.
leak4.fix1_html: Combine errands into one trip once or twice a week, and organise a carpool for school runs or commuting.
leak4.fix2: Check your tyre pressures monthly, and in cities with petrol price cycles, use a fuel price app to fill up near the bottom of the cycle.
leak4.fix3: Compare public transport fare caps and off-peak fares with what you spend on fuel and parking, and see if paying rego every 6 or 12 months suits you better than quarterly.
leak4.fix4_html: Get fresh quotes for car, home and contents insurance every year, and raise your excess only to a level your emergency fund can cover. Review your private health cover too, as premiums usually rise every April.

leak5.body_html: The daily flat white, the late-night online order, the "it was on special" purchase: impulse spending is the hardest leak to see because it never arrives as one bill. One-click checkout, saved card details and buy now, pay later remove the brief pause that would normally stop an unplanned purchase. When those purchases sit on a credit card charging around 20% interest a year, the leak grows: a $3,800 balance at 20.99% costs about $66 a month in interest alone.
leak5.fix1_html: Try the 24-hour rule: wait a full day before any non-essential purchase. Most urges fade.
leak5.fix2: Remove saved card details from shopping sites and turn off retailer notifications.
leak5.fix3_html: Pay the highest-interest debt first: pay the minimum on everything, and put every extra dollar towards the debt with the highest interest rate.
leak5.fix4: Consider a balance transfer card, but check the fee and the rate after the offer ends. If debt feels out of control, the free National Debt Helpline can help.

wealth.title: Turn Plugged Leaks Into Real Wealth
wealth.p1_html: Plugging leaks only matters if the money goes somewhere useful. The most powerful step is to automate the savings straight away. The same week you cut a bill, set up an automatic transfer for that exact amount into a high-interest savings account, your emergency fund, a mortgage offset account or a low-cost index fund. If the money never lands in your everyday account, it can't leak back out.
wealth.p2_html: Small amounts become large ones over time. Putting $300 a month into an investment averaging 7% a year could grow to roughly $52,000 in ten years and about $156,000 in twenty. Returns go up and down and are never guaranteed. Use the calculator above to try your own numbers, add only the ideas that fit your life, and switch on “Show in today’s money” to allow for rising prices.
wealth.p3: Start with one leak this week. Check your subscriptions tonight, compare your energy plan tomorrow, and plan next week's meals on Sunday. Each fix takes minutes, and the savings repeat every month.
